## Role of this chapter

- Institutional background (Colombian corporate tax system, 1980s) and data description that every later chapter leans on, so it isn't repeated in ch. 4-8.
- Two things downstream chapters cite directly: the juridical-organization split (corps = truth-reporters, used from @sec-testing onward) and the ST-liable/exempt industry split (used in @sec-fiscal).

Colombian manufacturing in 1981–1991 offers a unique setting to study tax evasion by overreporting deductible inputs. First, a sales tax that worked as a value-added tax and rewarded overreporting materials: manufacturers could reduce the tax they owed on their sales by claiming fictitious deductions (@sec-setting-incentive). Second, a truth-reporting group of firms: corporations, which government and market scrutiny kept from evading (@sec-setting-jo). Third, variation in the tax rate: the 1983 reform raised the sales-tax rate for most industries but left food products exempt (@sec-setting-st). Finally, firm-level records of output and inputs, together with legal form and taxes paid (@sec-setting-data). Because the approach uses the production function, it applies to any data with firms' output and inputs, such as surveys, administrative data, or tax records.

## Data {#sec-setting-data}

I use the Colombian Annual Survey of Manufacturing (EAM), a panel of manufacturing plants with more than 10 employees from 1981 to 1991.^[The survey's unit of observation is the plant; I refer to plants and firms interchangeably.] The EAM records, for each plant, the output and inputs that a production function needs, the plant's juridical organization, and the sales tax it charged on its sales and paid on its purchases.^[The year in the panel is the activity (reference) year. DANE runs the EAM each year with the economic year immediately preceding collection as the reference period [@DANE1995, p. 40]: the survey for year $x$ is collected during $x+1$ and labelled $x$ (e.g. the 1992–1994 surveys were collected in 1993–1995, and the 1992 file values assets at December 1992; @DANE2018).] The panel is well known: it has been used in seminal work on export dynamics, reallocation, and productivity, and to estimate production functions [@RobertsTybout1997; @Das2007; @Eslava2004; @Gandhi2020]. Similar to these studies, I observe inputs as firms reported them; in contrast, I ask how the tax incentives of the period, including the 1983 reform, shaped those reports. The working sample has 40,508 firm-years from 5,915 plants in 28 industries, covering the four juridical organizations described in @sec-setting-jo (@tbl-sum-stats).

![Summary statistics, manufacturing firms in Colombia (1981--1991).](/tables/ch03-summary-stats.png){#tbl-sum-stats}

## The sales tax: a credit on purchases {#sec-setting-incentive}

The Colombian sales tax worked as a value-added tax (VAT): manufacturers credited the tax paid on their purchases against the tax charged on their sales. The tax originally targeted the manufacturing sector, on finished goods and imports. From 1966, manufacturers could claim credit on the taxes paid on inputs *incorporated* into the product, and from 1974 on any purchase made by the firm, except the acquisition of capital goods; the credits worked through a system of refunds [@Perry1990, p. 180].

The credit rewards overreporting materials. An artificial increase in the reported value of materials raises the credit, and so lowers the firm's tax liability, by the tax rate paid on purchases, peso per peso. Capital goods could not be credited and labour was not a taxed purchase, so I focus on raw materials consumed.^[I exclude the other intermediates. Energy, fuels, and repair and maintenance are small, with medians of 1.0 percent, 0.3 percent, and 0.3 percent of gross output, and fuels and repair and maintenance are reported as zero in 8 and 15 percent of firm-years. Services, a median of 8.5 percent of gross output, entered the tax only gradually: the 1974 reform extended it to some services, and the 1983 reform to others, such as hotels, computing, maintenance, and rentals [@McLure1989, p. 65].]

Weak enforcement invited firms to collect this reward. Tax evasion flourished in Colombia during the sample period [@Sanchez1994], while the tax authority audited inefficiently, strained under its workload, and contended with legal loopholes [@Perry1990].

Food products (industries 311 and 312) offered almost no reward to overreporting, because they were exempt from the sales tax from its introduction [@Perry1990, p. 181]. Exempt firms charged no tax on their sales and, because the credits worked through a system of refunds [@Perry1990, p. 180], could claim back the tax they paid on purchases, but they paid almost none: the median rate on purchases was 0.2 percent in industry 311 and 0.6 percent in industry 312, against 9.2 percent in the liable industries. A fictitious peso of materials therefore saved these firms almost nothing. @sec-fiscal compares them with the liable industries.

## Juridical organizations: corporations as truth reporters {#sec-setting-jo}
<!-- continue editing here: Sep 27, 2026 -->
I treat corporations as truthful reporters of materials because two kinds of scrutiny restrained them from overreporting: government and market. First, the Superintendent of Corporations closely supervised corporations and required each to have an auditor, according to the OAS/IDB Joint Tax Program's *Fiscal Survey of Colombia* [-@FiscalSurveyColombia1965, pp. 27--30]; LLCs and proprietorships faced only the tax authority, whose audits were weak. Second, tradable shares subject corporations to market discipline, and the market penalizes aggressive tax behaviour even when it is legal. In the United States, stock prices fall, on average, when news of a corporation's involvement in tax shelters becomes public, although sheltering is avoidance rather than evasion [@HanlonSlemrod2009; @Slemrod2019]. If the market penalizes legal avoidance, it should penalize illegal overreporting at least as much. Evidence from Ecuador agrees: the tax evaded by claiming fictitious purchases amounted to 1.7 percent for corporations and 11.5 percent for sole proprietorships [@Carrillo2022]. If corporations nonetheless overreport, my estimates understate the overreporting of unincorporated firms; they are a lower bound.

The data distinguish several juridical organizations. Four of them account for 98 percent of firm-years and 95 percent of real gross output[^other-jo]: corporations, limited liability companies (LLCs), partnerships, and proprietorships (@tbl-jo-summary). I define them following the *Fiscal Survey of Colombia* [-@FiscalSurveyColombia1965, pp. 27--30] and DANE's documentation of the EAM [-@DANE2018, p. 12]. Corporations (*sociedades anónimas*) are associations of capital, the counterpart of the US corporation: at least five shareholders, tradable shares of equal value, and liability limited to the capital contributed [-@FiscalSurveyColombia1965; -@DANE2018]. An LLC (*sociedad de responsabilidad limitada*) has two or more partners, not exceeding 20 [-@FiscalSurveyColombia1965] or, by the 1990s, 25 [-@DANE2018], whose stakes (*cuotas*) cannot be traded and whose liability is limited to the capital contributed; it is an association of persons, not of capital, and is not subject to the Superintendent of Corporations unless more than one-third of it is owned by a corporation [-@FiscalSurveyColombia1965]. Partnerships are associations of two or more persons in which the partners, or at least the managing partners, are jointly, severally, and unlimitedly liable for the partnership's operations [-@DANE2018]. They are a small group (3.5 percent of firm-years), so I pool them with the other unincorporated firms. Proprietorships are individuals who run the business in their own name, without a separate legal personality [-@DANE2018].^[The *empresa unipersonal*, a single-owner legal entity, was introduced only in 1995 [@Ley2221995, art. 71].]

![Juridical organization, manufacturing firms in Colombia (1981--1991).](/tables/ch03-jo-summary.png){#tbl-jo-summary}

[^other-jo]: The other organizations in the data are excluded: stock partnerships (*sociedades en comandita por acciones*), whose shares are tradable and which are taxed as corporations [@FiscalSurveyColombia1965], and non-profit or state organizations, such as cooperatives, community enterprises, and state industrial enterprises, whose proceeds come from taxes, fees, or special contributions.

Because of the income tax, incentives to overreport varied within industries by juridical organization (@tbl-jo-rules). Firms could reduce their taxable profits and, with them, the income tax by deducting the cost of fictitious materials. Between 1974 and 1983, partnerships and LLCs paid a rate of 20 percent, and their owners paid individual income tax again on their share of the profits, whether distributed or not [@McLure1989, p. 67; @PerryCardenas1986, 1:23]. Proprietors paid only the individual income tax, on a graduated schedule with a top rate of 56 percent [@PerryCardenas1986, 1:36]. Corporations paid a rate of 40 percent between 1974 and 1986, and their shareholders paid individual income tax again only on the dividends they received [@McLure1989, p. 67; @PerryCardenas1986, 1:23]. Even though corporations had incentives to overreport too, the government and market scrutiny described above restrained them.


![Income tax, liability, capital, and owners by juridical organization (1974--1983).](/tables/ch03-jo-rules.png){#tbl-jo-rules}

## The 1983 reform {#sec-setting-st}

The 1983 reform altered the reward to overreporting across and within industries. Across industries, the reform raised the sales-tax rate in most liable industries and left exempt industries untouched. Within industries, it cut the income-tax rates by different amounts for each juridical organization: most for proprietorships, less for LLCs, and not at all for corporations. For unincorporated firms in liable industries, the two changes pulled in opposite directions: the higher sales tax raised the reward to overreporting, and the lower income tax reduced it. I exploit this variation in @sec-fiscal to test whether overreporting responded to its reward.

On the sales tax, the reform combined the items previously taxed at 6 and 15 percent into a single 10 percent bracket [@Perry1990, p. 182], while the exempt industries remained exempt. The typical taxed firm was in the 6 percent bracket, so the reform raised its rate: between 1983 and 1985, the median rate on sales rose from 6 to 10 percent, and the median rate on purchases, the rate at which each fictitious peso of materials was credited, from 6.6 to 9.9 percent (@tbl-st-by-year).

The new rate, set by Decreto 3541 of 29 December 1983 under the extraordinary powers of Ley 9 de 1983, applied from 1 April 1984 [@Decreto3541_1983; @CorteConstitucional2016; @Perry1990], so 1983 is the last full pre-reform year and 1984 a partial one. The observed rates match this timing (@tbl-st-by-year). The median rate paid on sales is 6 percent in 1981–1983, 10 percent from 1985, and 12 percent in 1991, after Ley 49 de 1990 raised the general rate to 12 percent [@Ley49_1990]. In 1984 it is 9 percent, exactly what three months at 6 percent and nine months at 10 percent give ($0.25\times6\%+0.75\times10\%=9\%$).

:::{#tbl-st-by-year}
![](/tables/ch03-st-by-year.png)

Observed sales-tax rates by survey year, on sales ($\tau_S$) and on purchases ($\tau_P$), against the statutory general rate in force. Rows in bold are the years a reform took effect: 1984 (Decreto 3541 de 1983, from 1 April) and 1991 (Ley 49 de 1990, from 1 January). Firms with a rate strictly between 0 and 50 percent.
:::

On the income tax, Ley 9 de 1983 cut the individual schedule, faced by proprietorships, by 4.6 percentage points on average, with the top rate falling from 56 to 49 percent, and the LLC rate from 20 to 18 percent [@PerryCardenas1986, 1:36].

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
**Draft block: the 1986 reform (Hans, 2026-09-26: kept in draft until deciding whether to open that door; all 1986 material lives here, @sec-fiscal only points to it).**

In 1986, Ley 75 cut income-tax rates again. It set the entity-level rate for corporations and LLCs at 30 percent, down from 40 percent for corporations and up from 18 percent for LLCs, and ended the double taxation of owners by exempting dividends and LLC profit shares from the individual income tax [@JunguitoRincon2004; @McLure1989, p. 67]. The individual schedule was reduced to four marginal rates, with a top rate of 30 percent. Because LLC owners had been taxed on all profits at the individual level, the combined marginal tax on an LLC's profits fell for most owners despite the higher entity-level rate; it rose only for owners in individual brackets below about 15 percent. The reform also moved the filing and collection of the income tax to the banking system [@JunguitoRincon2004; @Sanchez1994].
